meta.notice: Most evidence records are real publications whose DOI/PMID were checked against PubMed on 2026-11-25. This is a proof of concept: the products Radiance Serum and Clear Pore Serum and the three internal studies of them (no DOI/PMID) are invented so that every verdict can be demonstrated. They are listed in docs/RESEARCH_AND_ASSUMPTIONS.md.

ingredients.name: Purified Water
ingredients.description: Solvent and base component of most cosmetic emulsions and serums. Used to bring a formulation to 100%.
ingredients.solubility: Universal cosmetic solvent for water-soluble ingredients.

ingredients.name: Glycerin
ingredients.description: Widely used humectant that attracts and retains water in the stratum corneum.

ingredients.description: Vitamin B3 derivative studied for effects on the appearance of ageing facial skin. The cited clinical study tested a 5% niacinamide formulation; this is not a recommended or proven range for other formulas.

evidence.title: Niacinamide: A B vitamin that improves aging facial skin appearance
evidence.studyDesign: Double-blind, left-right randomised vehicle-controlled (split-face). Applied twice daily for 12 weeks; facial images and instrumental measures at baseline and 4-week intervals.
evidence.population: Female white subjects with clinical signs of facial photoaging
evidence.endpoint: Fine lines and wrinkles, hyperpigmented spots, red blotchiness, yellowing, elasticity (cutometry)
evidence.resultsSummary: Abstract reports significant improvements for niacinamide in fine lines and wrinkles, hyperpigmented spots, red blotchiness, skin yellowing and elasticity. The abstract does not state a percentage wrinkle reduction.
evidence.limitations: Ingredient-level (single 5% test vehicle), not the finished formulation. Single population (female, white). 12-week duration. Authors are affiliated with a cosmetics manufacturer.

evidence.title: Efficacy of cream-based novel formulations of hyaluronic acid of different molecular weights in anti-wrinkle treatment
evidence.studyDesign: Randomised, vehicle-controlled (periocular area, vehicle on the other eye). Twice-daily application for 60 days; measurements at baseline, 30 and 60 days.
evidence.population: Female subjects aged 30-60 with periocular wrinkles
evidence.endpoint: Skin hydration, elasticity, wrinkle depth (replica morphometry, Ra and Rz)
evidence.resultsSummary: All HA creams significantly improved hydration and elasticity vs placebo. Wrinkle depth improved significantly only for the 130 kDa and 50 kDa (low molecular weight) HA groups after 60 days.
evidence.limitations: Tested 0.1% hyaluronan creams; effect depends on molecular weight. Periocular area only. Not the finished formulation under assessment.

evidence.title: Niacinamide-containing facial moisturizer improves skin barrier and benefits subjects with rosacea
evidence.studyDesign: Randomised, investigator-blind, controlled observational study (untreated forearm control). Moisturizer applied twice daily to face and one forearm for 4 weeks; other forearm untreated.
evidence.testedSubject: A niacinamide-containing facial moisturizer (a different commercial formulation)
evidence.endpoint: Stratum corneum barrier function (instrumental and DMSO probe), hydration, rosacea severity
evidence.resultsSummary: The abstract states instruments provided objective measures of improved barrier function and hydration; it does not give numeric effect sizes.
evidence.limitations: Finished product is a different formulation with undisclosed niacinamide level. Population limited to rosacea. Observational design with untreated control.

evidence.title: Efficacy of a New Topical Nano-hyaluronic Acid in Humans
evidence.sourceName: Journal of Clinical and Aesthetic Dermatology
evidence.studyDesign: Open evaluation of a product range with instrumental and rater assessment (control not described in the abstract). Periorbital measurements over 8 weeks plus image rating by six trained raters.
evidence.testedSubject: A nano-hyaluronic acid product range (lotion, serum, cream) - a different commercial formulation
evidence.endpoint: Wrinkle depth (DermaTOP), hydration (Corneometer), elasticity (Cutometer), erythema
evidence.resultsSummary: Abstract reports significant moisturising effects after 2, 4 and 8 weeks and concludes wrinkle depth decreased by up to 40% and hydration increased by up to 96% at 8 weeks. The 'up to' figures are best-case values, not average effects.
evidence.limitations: Different formulation and undisclosed HA concentration. Small sample. Control group not described in the abstract. 'Up to' maxima overstate typical response.

evidence.title: New treatments for restoring impaired epidermal barrier permeability: skin barrier repair creams
evidence.studyDesign: Narrative review. Reviews the formulation and effect of skin barrier creams.
evidence.testedSubject: Barrier repair creams containing ceramides, hyaluronic acid and other substances
evidence.endpoint: Skin barrier repair (qualitative)
evidence.resultsSummary: Reviews externally applied substances such as ceramides and hyaluronic acid used to treat damaged skin barrier. The abstract is descriptive and gives no quantitative claim-level results.
evidence.limitations: Narrative review, no pooled quantitative estimate; cannot substantiate a specific numeric claim.

evidence.title: Ceramide-Containing Adjunctive Skin Care for Skin Barrier Restoration During Acne Vulgaris Treatment
evidence.studyDesign: Double-blind, controlled (ceramide cleanser + lotion vs basic cleanser). Participants used the acne gel once daily plus the ceramide routine or a basic cleanser twice daily; TEWL measured over 12 weeks.
evidence.population: Acne vulgaris patients treated with adapalene 0.3% / benzoyl peroxide 2.5% gel
evidence.testedSubject: A ceramide-containing foaming cleanser and facial lotion (different formulation)
evidence.endpoint: Transepidermal water loss (TEWL), dryness, lesion counts
evidence.resultsSummary: Abstract states TEWL in the ceramide group remained significantly lower than control at all timepoints and improved from baseline by week 12. No numeric TEWL percentage is given in the abstract.
evidence.limitations: Acne population with irritating drug treatment, not general dry skin. Different formulation and undisclosed ceramide level. Barrier damage was induced by the acne drugs.

evidence.title: Topical nicotinamide compared with clindamycin gel in the treatment of inflammatory acne vulgaris
evidence.studyDesign: Double-blind randomised comparison of 4% nicotinamide gel versus 1% clindamycin gel, applied twice daily for 8 weeks; Physician's Global Evaluation, lesion counts and acne severity rating at 4 and 8 weeks
evidence.population: Patients with moderate inflammatory acne vulgaris
evidence.endpoint: Inflammatory acne lesion counts (papules/pustules) and acne severity
evidence.resultsSummary: After 8 weeks 82% of patients on nicotinamide gel were improved on the Physician's Global Evaluation versus 68% on clindamycin (not significantly different, P=0.19). Papules/pustules fell by 60% with nicotinamide versus 43% with clindamycin (P=0.168) and acne severity by 52% versus 38% (P=0.161). The authors conclude 4% nicotinamide gel has comparable efficacy to 1% clindamycin gel.
evidence.limitations: Compared with an active drug, not with a vehicle control. Inflammatory acne in patients, not general blemish-prone skin. A 4% gel, not a finished cosmetic formula. Differences between the two treatments were not statistically significant.

evidence.title: The effect of 2% niacinamide on facial sebum production
evidence.sourceName: Journal of Cosmetic and Laser Therapy
evidence.studyDesign: Two trials. Japan: double-blind, placebo-controlled, 50 vs 50 subjects using a 2% niacinamide moisturizer for 4 weeks, sebum excretion rate (SER) at baseline, week 2 and week 4. USA: randomised split-face study in 30 Caucasian subjects for 6 weeks, SER and casual sebum level (CSL)
evidence.endpoint: Facial sebum excretion rate and casual sebum level
evidence.resultsSummary: In the Japanese study the 2% niacinamide group had significantly lower sebum excretion rate after 2 and 4 weeks. In the Caucasian study, after 6 weeks casual sebum level was significantly reduced but sebum excretion rate was not. The authors conclude 2% niacinamide may lower SER in Japanese individuals and CSL in Caucasian individuals. The abstract does not state a percentage reduction or pore-size change.
evidence.limitations: Measures sebum production, not pore appearance or pimples directly. Results differed between ethnic groups and between measures. Tested in a moisturizer at 2%, not the formula under assessment. Authors are affiliated with a cosmetics manufacturer.

evidence.title: The effect of niacinamide on reducing cutaneous pigmentation and suppression of melanosome transfer
evidence.studyDesign: In-vitro melanogenesis models plus two clinical trials: 18 subjects with hyperpigmentation using 5% niacinamide moisturizer vs vehicle in a paired design, and 120 subjects with facial tanning using vehicle, sunscreen, or 2% niacinamide + sunscreen; images analysed by computer and visual grading
evidence.population: Japanese women with facial hyperpigmentation or facial tanning
evidence.endpoint: Facial hyperpigmentation and skin lightness (image analysis)
evidence.resultsSummary: Niacinamide gave 35-68% inhibition of melanosome transfer in a coculture model. In the clinical studies niacinamide significantly decreased hyperpigmentation and increased skin lightness compared with vehicle after 4 weeks of use. It did not affect tyrosinase activity or melanogenesis in cultured melanocytes.
evidence.limitations: The 35-68% figure is an in-vitro result, not a clinical improvement. Japanese women only. Authors are affiliated with a cosmetics manufacturer. Clinical percentage improvement is not given in the abstract.

evidence.title: A Double-Blind, Randomized Clinical Trial of Niacinamide 4% versus Hydroquinone 4% in the Treatment of Melasma
evidence.studyDesign: Double-blind randomised split-face trial: 4% niacinamide cream on one side and 4% hydroquinone cream on the other for 8 weeks, with sunscreen; colorimetry, subjective scales and histology
evidence.endpoint: Skin colour (colorimetry), subjective improvement, histology
evidence.resultsSummary: All patients showed pigment improvement with both treatments and colorimetric measures did not differ between sides. Good to excellent improvement was seen in 44% with niacinamide versus 55% with hydroquinone. Niacinamide reduced mast-cell infiltrate and improved solar elastosis. Side effects occurred in 18% with niacinamide versus 29% with hydroquinone.
evidence.limitations: Small sample, melasma patients rather than general skin. Compared with hydroquinone, with no vehicle-only arm. Not a finished cosmetic formula.

evidence.title: Glycerol and the skin: holistic approach to its origin and functions
evidence.studyDesign: Narrative review of the effects, mechanisms and applications of glycerol in the skin
evidence.endpoint: Stratum corneum hydration, barrier function, mechanical properties
evidence.resultsSummary: The review reports that glycerol improves stratum corneum hydration, skin barrier function and mechanical properties, protects against irritating stimuli, and improves skin properties in xerosis and atopic dermatitis. It does not give a single quantified effect size.
evidence.limitations: Narrative review with no pooled quantitative estimate. Cannot substantiate a specific percentage or timeframe.

evidence.title: Glycerol accelerates recovery of barrier function in vivo
evidence.studyDesign: Two in-vivo studies measuring transepidermal water loss and capacitance: a 3-day follow-up after tape stripping, and a 7-day follow-up after repeated sodium lauryl sulphate washing; glycerol sites compared with untreated and base-treated sites
evidence.testedSubject: Glycerol applied to damaged stratum corneum
evidence.endpoint: Transepidermal water loss (barrier recovery) and stratum corneum hydration
evidence.resultsSummary: Barrier recovery was faster at glycerol-treated sites and stratum corneum hydration was higher, with differences still seen 7 days after treatment ended. The authors state the effects were based on modulation of barrier repair, not just the humectant effect.
evidence.limitations: Barrier-damage models (tape stripping, detergent), not normal skin. Sample size and glycerol concentration are not stated in the abstract. Short follow-up.

evidence.title: Skin moisturizing effects of panthenol-based formulations
evidence.studyDesign: Formulations with 0%, 0.5%, 1.0% or 5.0% panthenol applied daily to the forearms; skin moisture and TEWL measured before and after 15 and 30 days, plus effects after skin washing with sodium laureth sulphate
evidence.endpoint: Transepidermal water loss and skin moisture
evidence.resultsSummary: Formulations with 1.0% and 5.0% panthenol produced significant decreases in TEWL after 30 days of application. In skin washed with SLES, TEWL was significantly reduced two hours after applying panthenol formulations compared with control and vehicle. The authors conclude 1.0% panthenol improves protective effect on skin integrity.
evidence.limitations: Sample size not stated in the abstract. Forearm application on healthy skin. The abstract reports a TEWL decrease but no percentage.

evidence.title: In vivo efficacy and properties of semisolid formulations containing panthenol
evidence.studyDesign: Non-invasive in-vivo measurements over 48 hours on 40 women comparing o/w and w/o emulsions containing 5-13 wt% panthenol with the same formulations without panthenol; rheology and sensory evaluation
evidence.testedSubject: O/w and w/o emulsions with 5-13 wt% panthenol
evidence.endpoint: Skin hydration and transepidermal water loss
evidence.resultsSummary: After applying formulations containing 7-11 wt% panthenol, skin hydration increased and transepidermal water loss decreased, and skin pH shifted toward neutral.
evidence.limitations: Only a 48-hour observation window, so it says nothing about weeks of use. Effective range was 7-11 wt%, higher than the 1% often used in cosmetics.

evidence.title: A daily regimen of a ceramide-dominant moisturizing cream and cleanser restores the skin permeability barrier in adults with moderate eczema: A randomized trial
evidence.studyDesign: Randomised, placebo-controlled trial of a ceramide-dominant moisturizing cream and cleanser used daily for 28 days, assessed at baseline and every 7 days
evidence.testedSubject: A ceramide-dominant physiological-lipid moisturizing cream and cleanser (a different formulation)
evidence.endpoint: Transepidermal water loss, skin hydration, eczema severity score
evidence.resultsSummary: Transepidermal water loss and skin hydration improved significantly over time in the active group, while staying the same or worsening in placebo (P=.0342 and P<.0001). Eczema severity decreased in both groups with no significant difference between groups at day 28. Patient satisfaction (itch relief, dry skin, softness) was greater with the active product.
evidence.limitations: Population has eczema, not healthy dry skin. Different formulation with undisclosed ceramide level. Sample size not stated in the abstract. No numeric percentage change in the abstract.

evidence.title: Skin hydration is significantly increased by a cream formulated to mimic the skin's own natural moisturizing systems
evidence.studyDesign: Corneometry at baseline, 2, 4, 6 and 24 hours after a single application of a ceramide cream, compared with three reference moisturizers and placebo; TEWL after a single application; repeat insult patch and ophthalmologist/paediatric safety testing
evidence.testedSubject: A ceramide-containing moisturizing cream (a different formulation)
evidence.endpoint: Skin hydration (corneometry) over 24 hours and transepidermal water loss
evidence.resultsSummary: A single application of the ceramide cream significantly increased skin hydration (P<0.001), and at 24 hours hydration was significantly greater than for all three reference moisturizers. The placebo did not significantly increase hydration. TEWL decreased significantly over 24 hours, and the cream was non-sensitizing and non-irritating.
evidence.limitations: Single-application, 24-hour measurement: it does not show benefits after weeks of use. Different formulation with undisclosed ceramide level. Sample size not stated in the abstract.

evidence.title: Optimal ratios of topical stratum corneum lipids improve barrier recovery in chronologically aged skin
evidence.sourceName: Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology
evidence.studyDesign: Equimolar and cholesterol- or free-fatty-acid-dominant lipid mixtures (2% in propylene glycol/n-propanol) versus vehicle; barrier recovery after tape stripping measured up to 1 week in aged hairless mice and in aged human skin
evidence.population: Aged hairless mice and chronologically aged human skin (80 +/- 5 years)
evidence.testedSubject: 2% lipid mixture of cholesterol, ceramides and free fatty acids (3:1:1:1, cholesterol-dominant)
evidence.endpoint: Permeability barrier recovery rate after tape stripping
evidence.resultsSummary: A cholesterol-dominant 3:1:1:1 mixture further accelerated barrier recovery in aged mice at 3 and 6 hours, and significantly accelerated barrier recovery in aged human skin at 6 hours (p<0.005; n=6).
evidence.limitations: Very small human sample (n=6) in very old subjects. Tested a lipid mixture applied once, not cholesterol alone and not a finished product. 2% is the total lipid concentration.

evidence.title: Vitamin E: critical review of its current use in cosmetic and clinical dermatology
evidence.studyDesign: Critical review of cutaneous vitamin E research
evidence.endpoint: Antioxidant, photoprotective and skin barrier-stabilising properties
evidence.resultsSummary: The review states experimental evidence suggests topical and oral vitamin E has anticarcinogenic, photoprotective and skin barrier-stabilising properties, but that controlled clinical studies providing a rationale for indications and dosage are lacking. Its current use is largely limited to cosmetics.
evidence.limitations: Mostly experimental evidence; the authors explicitly note a lack of controlled clinical studies. Cannot substantiate a specific numeric claim.

evidence.title: Vitamin E in dermatology
evidence.studyDesign: Narrative review of cosmetic and clinical implications of vitamin E
evidence.endpoint: Free-radical scavenging and protection from solar radiation
evidence.resultsSummary: The review describes vitamin E as a fat-soluble antioxidant that protects skin from the effects of solar radiation by scavenging free radicals, and notes a paucity of controlled clinical studies supporting well-defined dosages and clinical indications.
evidence.limitations: Narrative review; the authors note few controlled clinical studies. No quantified effect.

evidence.title: Safety review of phenoxyethanol when used as a preservative in cosmetics
evidence.sourceName: Journal of the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology
evidence.studyDesign: Safety review of toxicological and clinical data on phenoxyethanol as a cosmetic preservative
evidence.endpoint: Safety and tolerability as a cosmetic preservative
evidence.resultsSummary: Per the European Scientific Committee on Consumer Safety, phenoxyethanol is safe for all consumers including children when used as a preservative at a maximum concentration of 1%. It has broad antimicrobial activity, is a rare sensitizer, and adverse systemic effects in animals occurred only at exposures about 200-fold higher than consumer exposure.
evidence.limitations: Safety evidence only: it says nothing about any skin-benefit claim. Applies to use as a preservative at up to 1%.

evidence.title: Improvement of naturally aged skin with vitamin A (retinol)
evidence.studyDesign: Randomised, double-blind, vehicle-controlled left-right arm comparison: 0.4% retinol lotion or vehicle applied up to 3 times a week for 24 weeks; clinical scoring (0-9) and skin biopsies
evidence.population: Elderly subjects (mean age 87) in senior-living facilities
evidence.endpoint: Fine wrinkling score and biochemical markers (glycosaminoglycan, procollagen I)
evidence.resultsSummary: After 24 weeks, fine wrinkling scores changed by -1.64 with retinol versus -0.08 with vehicle (P<.001) on a 0-9 scale. In subgroups, retinol significantly increased glycosaminoglycan expression (P=.02, n=6) and procollagen I immunostaining (P=.049, n=4).
evidence.limitations: Arms of very elderly subjects, not the typical cosmetic-user age. Effect reported as a score change on a 0-9 scale, not a percentage. 24 weeks, applied up to 3 times weekly.

evidence.title: Improvement of photoaged facial skin in middle-aged Japanese females by topical retinol (vitamin A alcohol): a vehicle-controlled, double-blind study
evidence.studyDesign: Randomised, blinded, vehicle-controlled half-face study using a once-nightly regimen: 26 weeks with 0.075% retinol cream in 57 subjects; a similar 13-week trial with 0.04% retinol cream
evidence.population: Middle-aged Japanese women with mild photoaging
evidence.testedSubject: 0.075% retinol cream (and 0.04% retinol cream for 13 weeks)
evidence.endpoint: Rate of improvement in fine and deep wrinkling
evidence.resultsSummary: After 26 weeks the rate of photoaging improvement was higher on the retinol side: fine wrinkling 50% (27 of 54) versus 24% (13) and deep wrinkling 28% (15 of 54) versus 2% (1). Three of 57 withdrew because of irritation. The 0.04% cream for 13 weeks gave less prominent improvement in fine wrinkling with minimal irritation.
evidence.limitations: Reports the share of subjects improving, not the percentage reduction in wrinkle depth. Japanese women only. Effect appeared over 13-26 weeks, not 4 weeks.

evidence.title: Treatment of acne vulgaris with salicylic acid pads
evidence.studyDesign: Review of four clinical studies (three placebo-controlled) and a comedolytic assay of 0.5% and 2% salicylic acid solutions applied as pads
evidence.population: Patients with mild to moderate acne vulgaris
evidence.endpoint: Number and severity of acne lesions; comedolytic activity
evidence.resultsSummary: In three placebo-controlled studies and a comedolytic assay, salicylic acid pads reduced the number of primary lesions and thereby the number and severity of all lesions. Comparative studies showed salicylic acid superior to benzoyl peroxide in reducing the total number of acne lesions. Adverse reactions were generally mild local irritation in a minority of patients.
evidence.limitations: 1992 review of older studies; the abstract gives no percentage reduction, sample sizes or study durations. Pad/solution format, not a finished serum.

evidence.title: Efficacy and safety of a facial serum and a mask containing salicylic acid and lipohydroxy acid in acne management: A randomized controlled trial
evidence.studyDesign: Randomised controlled trial, 1:1: facial serum plus mask versus serum alone for 8 weeks; acne severity, comedones, pores, tone evenness, sebum, hydration and TEWL assessed up to day 56
evidence.population: Adults in Shanghai with comedones, post-inflammatory erythema and/or hyperpigmentation
evidence.testedSubject: A serum and mask containing salicylic acid and lipohydroxy acid (a different formulation)
evidence.endpoint: Acne severity, skin pore density, sebum secretion, comedones, skin tone evenness, hydration
evidence.resultsSummary: After 8 weeks of treatment acne severity, density of skin pores, skin tone evenness, hyperpigmentation foci, closed and open comedones, sebum secretion and skin hydration were significantly improved from baseline in both groups (all p<0.05). Adding the mask further improved closed comedones and acne severity.
evidence.limitations: Both groups used the serum, so there was no untreated or vehicle control. Combination of salicylic acid and lipohydroxy acid, so the effect of salicylic acid alone cannot be isolated. Concentrations undisclosed. Improvements are reported as significant versus baseline without percentages in the abstract.

evidence.title: Vitamin C in dermatology
evidence.studyDesign: Narrative review of topical vitamin C in dermatology
evidence.endpoint: Photoageing and hyperpigmentation
evidence.resultsSummary: Vitamin C is described as a potent antioxidant that can be used topically to treat and prevent changes associated with photoageing and to treat hyperpigmentation. It is unstable and difficult to deliver into the dermis in optimum dosage, so research is directed at stable compounds and newer delivery methods.
evidence.limitations: Narrative review with no quantified effect or concentration in the abstract. Stability and delivery of ascorbic acid are flagged as problems.

evidence.title: Clinical, biometric and structural evaluation of the long-term effects of a topical treatment with ascorbic acid and madecassoside in photoaged human skin
evidence.studyDesign: Randomised double-blind study of topical 5% vitamin C with 0.1% madecassoside on photoaged skin for 6 months; clinical scores, elasticity measurements and histology of the elastic fibre network
evidence.endpoint: Wrinkles, suppleness, firmness, roughness, hydration, skin elasticity
evidence.resultsSummary: After 6 months the authors observed a significant improvement in the clinical score for deep and superficial wrinkles, suppleness, firmness, roughness and skin hydration, corroborated by elasticity measurements and histology. Two-thirds of subjects showed an improvement.
evidence.limitations: Vitamin C was combined with madecassoside, so the effect of vitamin C alone cannot be isolated. Small sample (20). Six-month duration. No percentage change in the abstract.

evidence.title: Urea: a comprehensive review of the clinical literature
evidence.studyDesign: Systematic literature review: PubMed search with 81 publications meeting inclusion criteria
evidence.population: Patients with dry and scaly skin conditions (review)
evidence.endpoint: Xerosis and other dry or scaly skin conditions
evidence.resultsSummary: Effective treatment with urea was reported for conditions including ichthyosis, xerosis, atopic dermatitis/eczema and psoriasis. Urea is described as a potent emollient and keratolytic agent. Mild irritation was the most common adverse event, with no systemic toxicity.
evidence.limitations: Review of heterogeneous clinical conditions, many of them medical. The abstract gives no concentrations or quantified moisturising effect for healthy skin.

evidence.title: Azelaic acid. A review of its pharmacological properties and therapeutic efficacy in acne and hyperpigmentary skin disorders
evidence.studyDesign: Review of pharmacology and controlled clinical studies of topical azelaic acid (usually a 20% cream)
evidence.population: Patients with acne and hyperpigmentary disorders such as melasma
evidence.endpoint: Comedonal and inflammatory acne; melasma and other hyperpigmentation
evidence.resultsSummary: Topical azelaic acid (usually 20% cream) was effective in comedonal and inflammatory acne. In controlled studies its anti-acne efficacy was comparable to topical tretinoin, benzoyl peroxide, erythromycin and oral tetracycline, and in melasma it was at least as effective as hydroquinone. Adverse effects were mild and transient local irritation.
evidence.limitations: 1991 review, drug-level 20% creams in patients, not a cosmetic concentration or finished cosmetic formula. No sample sizes or percentage effects in the abstract.

evidence.title: Squalane as a Promising Agent Protecting UV-Induced Inhibition of Collagen Biosynthesis and Wound Healing in Human Dermal Fibroblast
evidence.studyDesign: In-vitro study on human dermal fibroblasts exposed to UVA, measuring oxidative stress, collagen biosynthesis, inflammatory markers and migration in a wound-healing model
evidence.endpoint: UVA-induced oxidative stress, collagen biosynthesis, inflammation, fibroblast migration
evidence.resultsSummary: At 0.005-0.015%, squalane counteracted UVA-induced inhibition of collagen biosynthesis and oxidative stress, counteracted the UVA-induced increase in NF-kB and COX-2 (suggesting anti-inflammatory activity), and stimulated fibroblast migration in a wound-healing model.
evidence.limitations: Cell-culture study only: no human skin, no clinical endpoint. Cannot substantiate any consumer-perceivable benefit on its own.

evidence.title: 4-week vehicle-controlled brightening trial of Radiance Serum
evidence.studyDesign: Randomised, double-blind, vehicle-controlled study, serum applied twice daily for 4 weeks, skin tone evenness and brightness measured by colorimetry
evidence.endpoint: Skin tone evenness and brightness (colorimetry)
evidence.resultsSummary: skin tone evenness and brightness improved by 28% from baseline at week 4, significantly more than vehicle (p<0.01).
evidence.limitations: Single-site internal study; independent replication is advisable.

evidence.title: 8-week pore and blemish trial of Clear Pore Serum
evidence.studyDesign: Randomised, double-blind, vehicle-controlled study, serum applied twice daily for 8 weeks, pore appearance by image analysis, blemish counts and sebum excretion
evidence.endpoint: Visible pore appearance (image analysis), blemish counts, sebum
evidence.resultsSummary: visible pore appearance was reduced by 32% and blemish counts fell significantly versus vehicle at week 8; sebum excretion was also significantly lower.
evidence.limitations: Single-site internal study; independent replication is advisable.

evidence.title: Skin tone and brightness results from the 8-week Clear Pore Serum trial
evidence.studyDesign: Secondary endpoint of the same randomised, vehicle-controlled 8-week trial: skin tone evenness and brightness by colorimetry
evidence.endpoint: Skin tone evenness and brightness (colorimetry)
evidence.resultsSummary: no statistically significant change in skin tone evenness or brightness versus vehicle at week 4 or week 8. The serum improved pores and blemishes but not brightness.
evidence.limitations: Single-site internal study; independent replication is advisable.
